q: What is the atomic number of gold?
x: Gold's atomic number is 79, meaning each atom has 79 protons. Silver is 47, lead is 82 and copper is 29.

q: Which metal has the highest melting point of all metals, about 3,400 C?
x: Tungsten melts at about 3,422 C, which is why it was used for filaments in incandescent light bulbs.

q: Which moon of Jupiter is the most volcanically active body in the solar system?
x: Io is squeezed and stretched by Jupiter's gravity, which heats its interior and drives hundreds of active volcanoes.

q: Which moon of Saturn shoots plumes of water ice from cracks near its south pole?
x: The Cassini spacecraft flew through Enceladus's geysers, finding salty water and organic molecules.

q: Who discovered the planet Uranus in 1781?
x: Herschel first thought it was a comet. It was the first planet discovered with a telescope.

q: What is the SI unit of magnetic flux density?
x: The tesla honors Nikola Tesla. A typical MRI scanner uses a magnetic field of 1.5 to 3 tesla.

q: What is the SI unit of radioactivity, equal to one decay per second?
x: The becquerel is named after Henri Becquerel. One becquerel is very small, so large sources are measured in megabecquerels.

q: Which SI unit measures the absorbed dose of ionizing radiation?
x: One gray is one joule of radiation energy absorbed per kilogram of matter. It is named after physicist Louis Harold Gray.

q: What is the SI unit of electrical capacitance?
x: The farad is named after Michael Faraday. Most real capacitors are measured in microfarads or smaller.

q: What is the SI unit of inductance?
x: The henry is named after the American scientist Joseph Henry, who discovered self-induction in the 1830s.

q: Which SI base unit measures luminous intensity?
x: The candela was originally defined using the light of a standard candle, hence the name.

q: Which SI base unit measures the amount of a substance?
x: One mole contains exactly 6.02214076 x 10^23 particles, a number known as Avogadro's constant.

q: What is the freezing point of water on the Kelvin scale?
x: A change of one kelvin is exactly the same size as a change of one degree Celsius. The two scales differ only in their zero point.

q: Which part of the brain acts as the main relay station for sensory signals heading to the cortex?
x: Nearly all sensory information except smell passes through the thalamus on its way to the cerebral cortex.

q: Which cell organelle contains digestive enzymes that break down waste?
x: Lysosomes contain about 50 types of enzymes and work best in acidic conditions.

q: Which enzyme unwinds the DNA double helix before replication?
x: Helicase breaks the hydrogen bonds between base pairs, working like a zipper being opened.

q: Which nitrogenous base is found in RNA instead of thymine?
x: RNA uses uracil in place of thymine, and pairs it with adenine.

q: What is the medical name for the collarbone?
x: The clavicle is the most commonly broken bone in children. Its name comes from the Latin for little key.

q: What is the longest nerve in the human body?
x: The sciatic nerve runs from the lower back down each leg and is as thick as a finger.

q: Which of these is one of the three tiny bones of the middle ear?
x: The incus, malleus and stapes are also known as the anvil, hammer and stirrup, and they are the smallest bones in the body.

q: Vitamin B12 contains which metal ion at its center?
x: B12 is also called cobalamin because of the cobalt atom at its core. Only microorganisms can make it.

q: What is the most abundant protein in mammals?
x: Collagen makes up about a quarter of the protein in the human body and gives skin, tendons and bones their strength.

q: Which gas is the third most abundant in Earth's dry atmosphere, at about 0.9 percent?
x: Argon is produced mainly by the radioactive decay of potassium-40 in Earth's crust.

q: After oxygen, which element is the second most abundant in Earth's crust by mass?
x: Silicon makes up about 28 percent of the crust, mostly locked in silicate minerals and quartz.

q: What is the Mohs hardness of quartz?
x: Quartz is harder than steel and glass. Only topaz, corundum and diamond score higher on the scale.

q: Which scale has largely replaced the Richter scale for measuring large earthquakes?
x: The moment magnitude scale measures the total energy released and does not saturate for the biggest quakes.

q: Which type of seismic wave arrives first at a recording station?
x: P stands for primary. These compression waves travel through solids and liquids, while slower S-waves cannot pass through liquid.

q: In which hemisphere does the Coriolis effect deflect moving air to the right?
x: This deflection makes large storms spin counterclockwise in the Northern Hemisphere and clockwise in the Southern.

q: Which cloud type is responsible for thunderstorms?
x: Cumulonimbus clouds can tower more than 12 km high and are the only cloud type that produces thunder and lightning.

q: What is the boundary between the troposphere and the stratosphere called?
x: Commercial jets often cruise near the tropopause, where the air is smooth and thin.

q: In which atmospheric layer do most auroras occur?
x: Auroras glow roughly 100 to 300 km up, where charged particles from the Sun collide with oxygen and nitrogen.

q: Which spacecraft was the first to enter interstellar space, in 2012?
x: Voyager 1 was launched in 1977 and is the most distant human-made object from Earth.

q: Which star appears brightest in Earth's night sky, not counting the Sun?
x: Sirius, in the constellation Canis Major, is about 8.6 light-years away and is actually a pair of stars.

q: What will the Sun become after its red giant phase ends?
x: The Sun is too small to explode as a supernova. It will shed its outer layers and leave a dense core about the size of Earth.

q: What is the boundary around a black hole beyond which nothing can escape called?
x: The event horizon is not a physical surface. It is the point where the escape velocity equals the speed of light.

q: Which astronomer's observations in the 1920s showed that the universe is expanding?
x: Hubble found that distant galaxies are receding faster the farther away they are, and published the relation in 1929.

q: About how old is the universe?
x: The estimate comes from measurements of the cosmic microwave background and the expansion rate of the universe.

q: About how old is the Earth?
x: The age is derived from radiometric dating of meteorites and the oldest rocks, which give about 4.54 billion years.

q: What did Arno Penzias and Robert Wilson accidentally discover in 1964?
x: They first blamed the faint microwave hiss on pigeon droppings in their antenna. It turned out to be leftover radiation from the early universe.

q: Which particle carries the electromagnetic force?
x: Photons also make up visible light, and they have no mass or electric charge.

q: How many quarks make up a proton?
x: A proton contains two up quarks and one down quark held together by gluons.

q: Which European research organization operates the Large Hadron Collider?
x: The LHC's 27-kilometer ring lies beneath the border of France and Switzerland. The Higgs boson was found there in 2012.

q: Which scientist discovered electromagnetic induction in 1831?
x: Faraday showed that a changing magnetic field creates an electric current, the principle behind generators and transformers.

q: Who discovered in 1820 that an electric current produces a magnetic field?
x: Orsted noticed a compass needle twitch near a wire carrying current during a lecture demonstration.

q: Which physicist proposed in 1913 that electrons orbit the nucleus in fixed energy levels?
x: Bohr's model explained why hydrogen emits light only at specific colors.

q: Whose gold foil experiment showed that atoms have a small, dense nucleus?
x: A few alpha particles bounced almost straight back, which Rutherford compared to a shell bouncing off tissue paper.

q: Which element did Marie Curie name in honor of her homeland?
x: Curie announced polonium in 1898, naming it after Poland, which was then partitioned between three empires.

q: Which element with atomic number 99 is named after a famous physicist?
x: Einsteinium was first found in the debris of the 1952 hydrogen bomb test, and was kept secret for several years.

q: Which element is the most electronegative?
x: Fluorine pulls electrons so strongly that it reacts with almost every other element, including some noble gases.

q: What is the approximate pH range of human stomach acid?
x: Stomach acid is mostly hydrochloric acid, strong enough to dissolve some metals. A thick layer of mucus protects the stomach lining.

q: Which acid is used in lead-acid car batteries?
x: A lead-acid battery has plates of lead immersed in dilute sulfuric acid. The design dates from 1859.

q: Which noble gas has the lowest boiling point of all elements?
x: Helium boils at about -269 C, only 4 degrees above absolute zero, and never freezes at normal pressure.

q: Which is the lightest metal?
x: Lithium is so light that it floats on water, and it is used in rechargeable batteries.

q: The alloy bronze is made mainly of copper and which other metal?
x: The Bronze Age began around 3300 BC when people learned that adding tin made copper harder.

q: The alloy brass is made mainly of copper and which other metal?
x: Brass is bright and easy to shape, and its sound qualities make it the traditional material for horns.

q: Which naturalist independently came up with the theory of evolution by natural selection, prompting Darwin to publish?
x: Wallace sent Darwin his essay from the Malay Archipelago in 1858, and their ideas were presented together to the Linnean Society.

q: Which German chemist is said to have discovered the ring structure of benzene after a daydream?
x: Kekule said he envisioned a snake biting its own tail in 1865, which gave him the idea of a closed ring of carbon atoms.

q: Which French chemist is known as the father of modern chemistry and the law of conservation of mass?
x: Lavoisier named oxygen and hydrogen. He was guillotined during the French Revolution in 1794.

q: Which Danish astronomer used Jupiter's moons to estimate the speed of light in 1676?
x: Romer noticed that eclipses of Io ran late when Jupiter was farther from Earth, proving that light takes time to travel.

q: Which two Swiss astronomers discovered the first exoplanet orbiting a Sun-like star, in 1995?
x: Michel Mayor and Didier Queloz found 51 Pegasi b and shared the 2019 Nobel Prize in Physics for it.

q: Which Greek scholar estimated the Earth's circumference around 240 BC using shadows?
x: He compared the Sun's angle at two Egyptian cities and got a result within a few percent of the real value.

q: Whose experiments with swan-neck flasks helped disprove spontaneous generation?
x: In the 1860s, Pasteur showed that broth stayed clear as long as airborne germs could not reach it.

q: Which pair of Canadian researchers is credited with discovering insulin in 1921?
x: Frederick Banting and Charles Best worked in Toronto. Banting shared the 1923 Nobel Prize with J.J.R. Macleod.

q: Which mathematician described an abstract model of computation in 1936, now called a Turing machine?
x: Turing's model defined what it means for a problem to be computable. He also helped break the German Enigma code in World War II.

q: What does the abbreviation ASCII stand for?
a: American Standard Code for Information Interchange
Advanced System Code for Internet Integration
Automatic Symbol Coding for Input Interfaces
Applied Standard Computing and Information Interface
x: ASCII assigns numbers to letters and symbols. The original version used 7 bits, giving 128 characters.

q: How many bits long is an IPv4 address?
x: A 32-bit address allows about 4.3 billion unique addresses, which is why the longer 128-bit IPv6 was created.

q: The hexadecimal number system is base what?
x: Hexadecimal uses the digits 0 to 9 and the letters A to F. Programmers use it because one hex digit equals exactly four bits.

q: How many meters are in one international nautical mile?
x: A nautical mile equals one minute of latitude, and a speed of one nautical mile per hour is one knot.

q: What is the SI unit of electric charge?
x: One ampere of current is one coulomb of charge flowing past a point each second.

q: What is the approximate escape velocity from Earth's surface?
x: An object must travel at about 11.2 km/s to break free of Earth's gravity without further propulsion. That is more than 40,000 km/h.

q: What scattering effect makes the daytime sky blue?
x: Air molecules scatter short blue wavelengths much more strongly than long red ones, so blue light reaches your eyes from all directions.

q: Which gas law states that, at constant temperature, pressure and volume of a gas are inversely proportional?
x: Robert Boyle published his law in 1662. It explains why a scuba diver's lungs expand while ascending.

q: Which cell organelle makes lipids and has no ribosomes attached?
x: The smooth ER also helps detoxify chemicals, which is why liver cells have a lot of it.

q: To which biological kingdom do mushrooms belong?
x: Fungi are genetically closer to animals than to plants. They digest food outside their bodies and absorb it.

q: What term describes organisms that make their own food from simple substances?
x: Plants, algae and some bacteria are autotrophs. Most make food using sunlight, while others use chemical energy.

q: Jellyfish belong to which animal phylum?
x: Cnidarians, including jellyfish, corals and sea anemones, have stinging cells called cnidocytes.

q: Which bird is the fastest animal in a dive, exceeding 300 km/h?
x: Peregrine falcons have been clocked at over 320 km/h during their hunting dives, called stoops.

q: What is the largest cell in the human body?
x: The ovum is about 0.1 mm across and just visible to the naked eye. Sperm cells are among the smallest.

q: Which glands sit on top of the kidneys and release adrenaline?
x: The adrenal glands also make cortisol, the hormone linked with the body's response to stress.

q: Which muscle is the largest in the human body?
x: The gluteus maximus is the main muscle for standing up from a seated position and climbing stairs.

q: What are the two upper chambers of the heart called?
x: The atria receive blood returning to the heart, and the stronger ventricles pump it out.

q: Which flap of tissue covers the windpipe when you swallow?
x: The epiglottis closes over the airway during swallowing, so food and drink slide down the esophagus instead.

q: Which white blood cells produce antibodies?
x: B cells mature in bone marrow, which is where the B comes from in the older name bursa-derived. Each B cell makes just one type of antibody.

q: Which hormone, also called epinephrine, prepares the body for fight or flight?
x: Adrenaline speeds the heart, widens the airways and sends extra blood to the muscles within seconds.

q: Which English scientist first used the word cell for living things after viewing cork under a microscope in 1665?
x: Hooke thought the tiny compartments in cork resembled the small rooms, or cells, that monks lived in.

q: Which three American physicists invented the transistor at Bell Labs in 1947?
x: The transistor replaced bulky vacuum tubes and made modern electronics possible. The trio shared the 1956 Nobel Prize in Physics.

q: The Haber process is used to industrially produce which compound?
x: The Haber process combines nitrogen from the air with hydrogen, making the fertilizer that helps feed billions of people.

q: What is the approximate temperature at the Sun's core?
x: At the core, hydrogen nuclei fuse into helium, releasing the energy that powers the Sun.

q: What is the larger of Mars's two moons?
x: Phobos orbits so close to Mars that it circles the planet three times a day and is slowly spiraling inward.

q: Which large moon of Neptune orbits in the opposite direction to the planet's rotation?
x: Triton's backward orbit suggests it was captured from the Kuiper Belt. It has nitrogen geysers and is one of the coldest known places in the solar system.

q: What was the name of the lander that touched down on comet 67P in 2014?
x: Philae was carried by the European probe Rosetta and made the first soft landing on a comet.

q: How many hexagonal mirror segments make up the James Webb Space Telescope's primary mirror?
x: The segments are coated in a thin layer of gold, which reflects infrared light well. The mirror unfolded after launch.

q: What is the average distance from Earth to the Moon?
x: Light takes about 1.3 seconds to travel from the Moon to Earth.

q: Roughly how long is one astronomical unit, the average distance from Earth to the Sun?
x: One astronomical unit is about 150 million km, or 93 million miles. Neptune orbits at about 30 AU.

q: What is Avogadro's number, approximately?
x: It is the number of particles in one mole of a substance. 12 grams of carbon-12 contain this many atoms.

q: Which subatomic particle in an atom has the least mass?
x: A proton is about 1,836 times heavier than an electron.

q: Which element makes up the largest share of the human body's mass?
x: Oxygen is about 65 percent of body mass, mostly because the body is so rich in water. Carbon is next at about 18 percent.

q: What is the longest phase of the cell cycle called?
x: Cells spend most of their lives in interphase, growing and copying their DNA, and only a small fraction of time dividing.

q: Which British chemist isolated sodium and potassium by electrolysis in 1807?
x: Davy reportedly danced around his lab with joy when he saw tiny globules of potassium form and burst into flame.

q: Which Greek letter is the standard symbol for wavelength in physics?
x: Wavelength, written as lambda, multiplied by frequency gives the speed of a wave.
